intro.title: Why this tour
paragraphs: On Juneteenth, Barack Obama opened his presidential center in Jackson Park, on the same ground where Chicago held the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. The fair called itself the White City, while Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass stood at its gates distributing a pamphlet titled "The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition." Today, words from the first Black president appear across a 225-foot tower on that ground.

The two summers were very different. The fair was built for one season of paying visitors, and **its organizers excluded Black Americans from its exhibits and most of its jobs**. **The Center was built for the surrounding community and, in large part, by people from that community**. This walk explains how that change took place.

Paul Cornell bought 300 acres along the lakefront in 1853, arranged for the Illinois Central to build a train stop, and marketed Hyde Park to wealthy Chicagoans as a place to escape the city. **From the beginning, the neighborhood was designed around exclusivity**. The University of Chicago opened in 1892, followed by the fair the next summer.

As Black families moved north during the Great Migration, Hyde Park's exclusivity became formal policy. **In 1917, the Chicago Real Estate Board adopted a block-by-block segregation policy**. In 1924, the national realtors' association added the same idea to its code of ethics, and **in 1927 its counsel drafted a racially restrictive covenant and promoted it throughout Chicago**. Hyde Park property owners readily adopted the covenants. **The University of Chicago spent more than $80,000 defending them in court**, and in 1928 the Hyde Park Herald praised the covenants for surrounding the neighborhood like a "marvelous delicately woven chain of armor." When Carl Hansberry bought a home near Washington Park in 1937, neighbors sued him under one of those covenants. His daughter Lorraine later used that experience in **A Raisin in the Sun**, the first play by a Black woman produced on Broadway.

The methods changed over time. **Banks and the Federal Housing Administration redlined Black neighborhoods**, while **speculators bought homes cheaply from white owners and resold them to Black families at twice the price through contracts that provided no equity**. **Duke researchers estimate that these buyers lost between $3 billion and $4 billion**. Hyde Park later used another method. The University of Chicago created the South East Chicago Commission in 1952 to manage integration, and that work relied heavily on demolition. **The 1958 urban renewal plan displaced about 4,000 families, most of them Black and poor**. In 1963, James Baldwin summarized the policy by saying that urban renewal meant Negro removal.

These changes were not accidental. **Each policy was created, approved, and carried out by specific people and institutions**. Understanding that history matters because **policies made by people can also be changed by people**.

The Center represents a different approach. **Lakeside Alliance, a construction team led by four Black-owned Chicago firms, built it** with a goal of awarding as much as half of more than $300 million in subcontracts to diverse businesses. The campus also adds public spaces and services to the neighborhood, including a new Chicago Public Library branch, a fruit and vegetable garden, a playground, and the sledding hill Michelle Obama requested. The fair charged fifty cents for admission, while the Great Lawn is open free every day.

In 1893, Black Chicagoans were told that they had no place in the future represented on this ground. On Juneteenth, the Center sent a different message. This walk covers both the policies that created exclusion and the efforts now being made to address their effects.

I started Rooted Forward after learning that **many people, including longtime Chicago residents, had never been taught this history**. Students research and write these tours, and we provide them free because history has little effect when people do not know it.
intro.byline: Zain Zaidi is a sophomore at the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools and the founder of Rooted Forward, a youth-led nonprofit documenting Chicago's history of housing discrimination.

practical.title: Getting there and timing
practical.text: The walk starts at East 53rd Street and South Shore Drive, in the south end of Harold Washington Park, across from the Hampton House at 5300 South Shore Drive, and ends at Harper Court, two blocks from where it began. The stops run in time order rather than in a neat loop, so the route doubles back on itself and a few stops sit within sight of each other. Plan on about three hours with the stops. The 53rd Street Metra station is a six-minute walk west of the start and a block from the finish. Short on time? Stop after the Obama Center, five stops in, and save the university for another day.

practical.title: The ground
practical.text: Flat city sidewalks the whole way, about four miles on the main line. The longest single leg is the eighteen minutes from the tracks down to Jackson Park. The busiest crossings are on 57th Street, along Stony Island, and at Lake Park; use the marked crosswalks. The university quadrangles are open to walk through every day. Going inside Robie House takes a timed ticket, but this tour only needs the outside.

practical.title: The three detours
practical.text: Stops twelve, thirteen and fourteen are drawn in green on the map because they are genuinely out of the way. **Do them in daylight, and take someone with you if you can.** The Hansberry house and Daley's sit southwest of campus in Woodlawn, and Drexel Boulevard runs northwest through Kenwood, so the three of them cross the neighborhood from top to bottom, and the legs between them are long and residential. All three add roughly two hours on foot. The Hansberry house is where the covenant wall first cracked, Daley's is by most accounts the oldest restaurant in the city, and Drexel is where you can read this whole tour in one street. The number 4 bus runs the length of Cottage Grove past Daley's and Drexel Square both, and the Green Line stops at 63rd. The main walk is complete without any of them.

practical.title: Listening
practical.text: Headphones are nicest, but a phone speaker works fine. Every stop's audio is also printed on the page, so you can read instead of listen. If you share your location, it is used only to draw your dot on the map. It never leaves your phone.

tour.detourNotice: This optional stop is separated from the main route and requires additional walking time. **Visit during daylight and, when possible, travel with another person.** The route includes long residential sections with fewer pedestrians than 53rd Street or the university campus. Completing all three detours adds about two hours of walking, although the number 4 Cottage Grove bus covers much of the distance. The main route contains the complete central story, so the detours can be skipped without losing the tour's main sequence.

stops.title: Paul Cornell's stone
stops.dek: A stone in the park marks the approximate starting point of Hyde Park
transcript: Find the boulder in Harold Washington Park at East 53rd Street and South Shore Drive, across from the tall brick building with the black awning. That building will become important shortly. The stone stands near the place where Hyde Park began. Before continuing, look at the towers on this block and the trains behind the trees. Both trace back to a farm that a lawyer bought near this location in 1853.

Paul Cornell was a young lawyer from upstate New York who arrived in Chicago in 1847 with one dollar and fifty cents. A thief stole his belongings on his first night in the city, so he had to begin again with almost nothing. He later met Illinois senator Stephen Douglas, who advised him to invest south of Chicago because the city was likely to grow in that direction. Cornell eventually rode south along the lake shore, through marsh grass and sand ridges, until he reached a small farm and tavern near present-day 53rd Street. It served travelers making the final part of their trip into Chicago.

**In August 1853, Cornell bought sixty acres from Electa Watson Garnsey, the tavern keeper's widow**. **He continued buying land until he owned about 300 acres of lakefront between roughly 51st and 55th Streets**. He named the area Hyde Park to give it a refined image. At the time, Chicago sent sewage into the river and lake and was known for its smell. Cornell marketed Hyde Park as an escape with cleaner air and cooler water for families who could afford to leave the city.

Cornell needed a reliable way to bring those families to Hyde Park. In 1856, he gave the Illinois Central sixty acres of land at no cost. In return, **the railroad built a station at 53rd Street and guaranteed daily trains downtown**. On the first run, June 1, 1856, the station agent reported that there was not a single passenger up or down. Regular service still began that July, with four trains each day at a fare of seven and a half cents. The line later became extremely busy, carrying more than five hundred trains a day by 1929. Cornell divided his property into large lots, with eighteen lots per block and fifty feet of frontage, and kept the development relatively rural. Early residents maintained gardens, stables, and some animals.

**Cornell built the Hyde Park House on the shore as the center of the resort**. The hotel stood between the water and the railroad and hosted concerts, parties, and political dinners. Mary Todd Lincoln stayed there for two and a half months after her husband's assassination. The hotel burned in 1877. A generation later, the Sisson Hotel was built on this part of the shore. The brick tower in front of you is that building, now called the Hampton House.

Look east and notice how far the lake is from this corner. The tennis courts out there are close to where the water once stopped. A person standing in 1858 where 53rd Street meets South Shore Drive would have been in the water. A breakwater extended north from the corner and formed a small harbor. When the Sisson opened in 1918, the beach began across a narrow lakefront street. **Everything east of you now is manufactured ground.** In 1919, the City Council approved filling the south lakefront under Burnham's 1909 plan, and Chicago voters approved twenty million dollars for the project in February 1920. Crews began placing fill at 12th Street and reached 55th Street by 1924. A road opened on the new land in 1929 as Leif Erickson Drive and was renamed Lake Shore Drive in 1946.

The Sisson Hotel also has a record of exclusion. **The Ku Klux Klan operated openly in Hyde Park during the 1920s and printed its weekly newspaper on 55th Street**. The American Unity League, a Catholic organization in Chicago, responded by publishing the names of Klan members. The list included Harry Sisson, the hotel's proprietor. Catholic and Jewish guests stopped coming, and the hotel never recovered its earlier business. Sisson sold the property, which was later renamed the Sherry and then the Hampton House. Its ballroom later hosted Duke Ellington and Jewish weddings, and Harold Washington lived in the building beside the park now named for him. Cornell had marketed the lakefront to wealthy families who could leave the city. Sisson made clear which other families were unwelcome, and later stops show the same exclusion written into property deeds.

stops.title: The Del Prado
stops.dek: A surviving hotel from Hyde Park's resort period
transcript: **The apartment building on this corner opened in 1918 as the Cooper-Carlton Hotel**. Near the top, carved faces appear in the terra cotta. The owners included them because they claimed a family connection to novelist James Fenimore Cooper. **In 1930, the building took the name Del Prado from an older hotel on the Midway** that was being demolished for International House. Stop six is located on the site of that earlier hotel.

During this period, Hyde Park operated as a resort district, and this corner served as one of its main entrances. Some families stayed for the entire summer and rented large suites or even a full floor. Each morning, the men took Cornell's trains downtown to work, while the rest of the family spent the day at the beach, in the parks, sailing near the Point, eating in restaurants, or attending concerts in hotel ballrooms. Before air travel became common, vacations were usually closer to home, and railroads actively promoted destinations such as Hyde Park.

The Illinois Central promoted Hyde Park to travelers far beyond Chicago. Its main line continued south through Mississippi to New Orleans, and advertisements encouraged families from the Midwest and the South to spend the summer beside Lake Michigan. Trains were the fastest form of long-distance travel, and Hyde Park was directly connected to the line.

The building now contains apartments, and its interior has been restored. You can enter the lobby to see the ceilings or examine the arches from the sidewalk. In the hotel's busiest years, trunks would have been stacked along the curb, porters would have carried enough luggage for an entire season, and music might have been coming from an upstairs ballroom.

The families staying at this hotel were white, as were the names on the deeds along the boulevards. Many of the workers who carried luggage and prepared meals were not. Hyde Park's small Black community lived about two blocks west, close to the railroad embankment. The next stop is on that street.

stops.title: The tracks and Lake Park
stops.dek: The railroad served downtown Chicago and the South
transcript: The railroad tracks in front of you made Hyde Park's development possible. Cornell's agreement created a station at 53rd Street in 1856, and commuter trains have stopped here continuously for about 170 years. In 1926, the Illinois Central electrified the line after the city ordered changes to its four hundred daily coal-burning engines. Metra still uses the same embankment. Although the line is often understood as a connection between Hyde Park and downtown, its main route also continues south through Mississippi to New Orleans.

**During the Great Migration, that north-south route helped change the country.** Black southerners traveled north on the Illinois Central in two major waves, one around the World Wars and another afterward. Hundreds of thousands moved toward factory work and away from violence and oppression in the South. The Chicago Defender, the city's leading Black newspaper, traveled south on the same trains in the bags of porters and urged readers to leave what it called the land of suffering. Many migrants arrived at Illinois Central stations only a few miles from this spot. They became essential to Chicago's industrial workforce, while most city neighborhoods, including Hyde Park, refused to allow them to live there.

Lake Park Avenue was the working side of Cornell's resort. The land along the tracks fell under railroad jurisdiction and was outside the village's restrictions on alcohol, so many saloons opened here. In one year during the 1870s, the village approved forty-nine saloon licenses and rejected only one. Coal yards, stables, and inexpensive frame buildings were also concentrated along this corridor, providing the services needed to keep the resort operating.

This area was also home to Hyde Park's Black residents. In the early 1900s, a small **middle-class Black community lived along Lake Park and Harper avenues**, close to the tracks. The neighborhood included an AME church on Lake Park, a colored Republican Club, and a social column in the Chicago Defender. The 1900 census lists Black cooks and waiters who worked in the hotels, many born in Kentucky, Tennessee, and Mississippi. They lived near white pipe welders and Chinese laundry owners. In 1914, the Half Century Club held a reception at Rosalie Music Hall for Booker T. Washington, then the most prominent Black leader in the country. At the same time, the rest of Hyde Park remained almost entirely white and actively tried to preserve that separation.

The arrangement visible here appeared throughout Hyde Park. The boulevards formed the neighborhood's public face, while Black residents were concentrated near the tracks. No law yet required that pattern. It had developed over several decades before formal rules were written, and the next stops explain how Hyde Park marketed itself while maintaining that separation.

stops.title: The White City
stops.dek: The park came before the fair and later became a major site of exclusion
transcript: You are standing in Jackson Park. The domed building across the water is **the only major palace from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition that remains on its original site**. The fair is better known than the park, but the park was developed first and made it possible to hold the exposition here. The history of the site begins with the land itself.

Paul Cornell spent about two decades working to establish large public parks on the South Side. It took money to do that. **The campaign was run by landowners whose property the parks would make valuable, and Cornell held three hundred acres beside the ground he was asking the state to improve.** He and his supporters began promoting a park bill in 1866. Voters rejected the first proposal, and Cornell traveled to Springfield during two consecutive winters to support a later version. **The law passed on February 24, 1869, and the new commissioners selected land for the parks**. **They chose 1,055 acres of sandbar, marsh, and open water about six miles south of downtown**, including the land around you. **They then hired Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, the designers of Central Park**.
Their 1871 plan is shown on this page. It proposed one park along the lake, another park one mile west, and a landscaped channel connecting them.

The table in the left margin gives the size of the plan. **Its 1,055 acres were divided into an Upper Division of 372 acres, a Midway Division of 90 acres, and a Lower or Lagoon Division of 593 acres.** The Upper Division became Washington Park and remains 372 acres. The Lagoon Division is the land around you. The Midway Division connects the two parks. Olmsted planned to place **water down the middle of it**, allowing boats to enter from Lake Michigan, cross the lagoon, and reach a landing in Washington Park. The plan also included fourteen miles of drives, thirty miles of walking paths, and 1.6 miles of lakefront. At the time, the parks were simply parts of one South Park. The commission invited public suggestions and named them Jackson Park and Washington Park in 1881.

Olmsted's report described the land in detail. He considered its flatness the site's first major problem and explained that the lake had gradually formed this area as a sandbar. **Across the full 1,055 acres, he found no more than a dozen small dwellings**. Washington Park was built largely according to the plan, including a one-hundred-acre lawn called the Southopen Green, where sheep grazed to keep the grass short. Jackson Park was not completed as planned.

The Great Chicago Fire in October 1871 destroyed the park drawings as well as county land records needed for the commission's condemnation cases. City funds were redirected toward rebuilding. The following year, designer Horace Cleveland was hired to complete the work that could still be afforded, mainly paths and plantings rather than the major excavation required for the water system. Washington Park developed during the next two decades, while Jackson Park remained mostly unfinished. That open, publicly owned lakefront land later made it attractive for the World's Fair. After Chicago defeated New York, Washington, and St. Louis for the exposition, planners needed hundreds of acres near rail lines. Daniel Burnham selected Jackson Park, and Olmsted returned in old age to reshape land he had planned decades earlier, including the creation of the Wooded Island from the sandbar. Nearby land values began rising as soon as the site was announced.

The scale of the fair was intended to match the world's largest expositions. Paris had recently produced the Eiffel Tower, and Chicago wanted to demonstrate its recovery less than twenty years after the Great Fire. Daniel Burnham directed architects who completed a large complex of monumental buildings in about two years. **Although photographs make the buildings look like carved stone, most were steel frames covered in plaster**. Painting them all white created a consistent appearance and led newspapers to call the site the White City. Extensive electric lighting made the grounds especially striking at night and drew visitors for both the illumination and the exhibits.

The fair operated from May 1 through the end of October and received about **27 million visits in a country with 65 million people**. On one day in October, 761,000 people entered the grounds. Visitors saw products including the dishwasher, the zipper, and Juicy Fruit gum, as well as the large wheel designed by bridge engineer George Ferris. The fair also promoted a harmful racial stereotype. A food company hired **Nancy Green, a Chicago woman who had been born into slavery in Kentucky**, to prepare pancakes while dressed as Aunt Jemima, a fictional plantation cook used to advertise flour. The character was popular with visitors and presented the Old South as pleasant and harmless.

Black Americans were excluded from the fair's planning, exhibit halls, and nearly all of its jobs. **Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass** responded by distributing The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition at the gates. The pamphlet included prefaces in English, French, and German so international visitors could understand its argument. Wells distributed thousands of copies. Douglass, then in his seventies, worked from the Haiti Pavilion, the only building that prominently presented Black achievement, because Haiti had appointed him as its commissioner. Fair organizers offered only one Colored American Day late in the summer, when Douglass delivered a major speech.

Much of the White City was destroyed soon after the fair. A fire in January 1894 burned the Casino, Peristyle, and Music Hall and killed firefighter William Mackie. On July 5, during the Pullman strike, another fire near the Terminal Station destroyed seven major buildings while about one hundred thousand people watched. The Chicago Tribune blamed boys who had been playing in the ruins. Buildings that did not burn were generally dismantled and removed. The domed structure in front of you survived because it contained borrowed art and the lenders required fireproof construction. **Charles Atwood therefore designed it with a brick and steel frame**, although its exterior was covered in plaster like the other fair buildings.

Several parts of the fairgrounds remain. During the 1930s, the building in front of you was rebuilt with about 28,000 tons of Indiana limestone cut to reproduce Atwood's original details. It has operated as a science museum since 1933 and was renamed the **Kenneth C. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry** in 2024. The Columbia Basin in front of it is the remaining section of the fair's north lagoon. The arched bridge across the basin was named for Clarence Darrow in 1957 and has been closed by fencing since 2013 while the city plans its reconstruction. South of the basin is Olmsted's Wooded Island. **Japan built a temple pavilion called the Ho-o-den there for the fair**. It remained for about fifty years, was boarded up after Pearl Harbor, and was destroyed by arson in 1946. A Japanese garden opened on the island in 1981, was named Osaka Garden in 1993, and received Yoko Ono's installation of twelve steel lotus petals in 2016 on the former pavilion site.

At the south end of the park, **the Statue of the Republic stands near the former location of the fair's Administration Building**. The current statue is a 24-foot bronze created by Daniel Chester French in 1918. It is one-third the size of the original gilded plaster statue, which park commissioners intentionally burned in 1896. The bronze is currently surrounded by scaffolding for its first regilding since 1992. That restoration is being funded as one of the conditions connected to construction of the Obama Presidential Center, the next stop about ten minutes south. As you continue, remember the title of Wells and Douglass's pamphlet, which raised the central question of who the fair and its vision of progress were meant to include.

stops.title: The Obama Center
stops.dek: A deliberate break from the tour's chronological order
transcript: The tour is arranged chronologically, but this stop is an exception. Every later stop covers events before 2026. The Center appears here because its location and meaning are closely connected to the 1893 fairgrounds, which stood about a quarter mile north across the water.

Stand on the plaza where the full tower is visible. Near the top, lines from Barack Obama's 2015 Selma speech are carved into the granite. **The museum opened on June 19, 2026, Juneteenth**. Construction took nearly five years and cost about 850 million dollars. The Obamas selected Jackson Park, the same area where Chicago held the World's Columbian Exposition. The surrounding South Side neighborhoods also helped launch the careers of Harold Washington, Chicago's first Black mayor, and Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected to the United States Senate, before Barack Obama became president.

The Center differs sharply from the fair built here in 1893. The White City was constructed quickly for one season of paid admission, and Black Americans were excluded from its halls and most of its jobs. The Center was built by **Lakeside Alliance, a construction team led by four Black-owned Chicago firms**, with a goal of awarding as much as half of more than 300 million dollars in subcontracts to diverse businesses. Unlike the fenced fairgrounds, the Center is part of a public park. **The campus includes a new Chicago Public Library branch, a fruit and vegetable garden, a playground, and a sledding hill requested by Michelle Obama**. These facilities were designed for the communities that the fair excluded.

Construction of the Center also included funding and requirements for improvements elsewhere in Jackson Park. The federal review that approved the project required the Statue of the Republic to be regilded for the first time since 1992, the historic English Comfort Station to be rehabilitated, and the park's history to be presented to visitors. In this way, a project completed in 2026 is helping repair features that date to the 1893 fair.

The Center has also increased concerns about housing costs in the surrounding neighborhoods. In May 2026, the Hyde Park Herald published an Illinois Answers Project report on changes near the campus. **Median rents in the area had risen about 43 percent since the Center was announced in 2015, compared with roughly 14 percent across Chicago**. The median sale price of a single-family home in East Woodlawn **doubled from 2019 to 2025, reaching $440,000**. **In 2020, the city passed the Woodlawn Housing Preservation Ordinance, which reserved 52 city-owned lots for affordable housing** and funded seven programs intended to help residents remain in place. Five years later, one 58-unit development had opened with 41 affordable apartments. Thirty-six homeowners had received repair grants of about twenty thousand dollars each, while about **two million dollars remained unspent**.

This raises a central question for the neighborhood. For about seventy years, the policies discussed later in this tour limited investment in these blocks. Investment is now returning, but longtime residents are concerned that they may not be able to remain for the next decade. The outcome will depend on local decisions, including ward meetings, housing ordinances, and public participation, rather than on the Center alone.

The tour now returns to the earlier history of Hyde Park. The remaining stops explain how the neighborhood was developed. The next stop is a few hundred yards west at the site of a hotel that opened in the same spring as the fair.

stops.title: The first Del Prado
stops.dek: The site of a fair-era hotel later became International House
transcript: The Gothic building facing the Midway is International House. It stands on the site of the hotel that gave stop two its later name. **In April 1893, shortly before the fair opened, a buff-brick hotel called the Raymond and Whitcomb Grand was completed here**. It had four stories, 325 rooms, and another 62 rooms in an annex. Its main feature was a **250-foot verandah facing the Midway**, where guests could eat breakfast while watching the crowds and attractions. The hotel was soon renamed the Del Prado.

Hotels opened throughout Hyde Park for the 1893 fair. The Del Prado, Chicago Beach, and Windermere offered amenities that guests considered modern, including hot and cold running water, steam heat, electric lights, and telephones. To carry the crowds, the Illinois Central raised its tracks onto the embankment crossed earlier in the tour and transported an estimated four million riders during the fair's six-month run. The hotels remained after the exposition and made this area one of the country's best-known resort hotel districts for the next generation.

By 1930, the Del Prado had declined and its large verandah had been enclosed. **The University of Chicago purchased the property, demolished the hotel, and built International House** with Rockefeller funding as a residence for students from many countries. The Del Prado name was transferred to the Cooper-Carlton Hotel on 53rd Street, which still uses it.

This block shows a pattern that would occur repeatedly near the university. An older neighborhood institution declined, the university purchased the property, and a Gothic campus building replaced it. The change here also contained a contradiction. The Del Prado had served mainly white travelers, while International House was created so students from around the world could live together. At the same time, the surrounding neighborhood was using formal restrictions to exclude Black Chicagoans living only a mile west. Both developments occurred on the same site.

stops.title: The Midway line
stops.dek: A planned canal became a long-standing neighborhood boundary
transcript: During the fair, this mile-long strip was the main entertainment area. The formal White City stood to the east, while the Midway contained beer gardens, musical performances, sideshows, and restaurants representing many countries. **Its largest attraction was the first Ferris wheel, a 264-foot structure designed as an American response to the Eiffel Tower**. A fifty-cent ticket provided two slow rotations lasting about twenty minutes. The Midway attractions earned millions of dollars, and the term midway later became the common name for carnival entertainment areas. After the fair, crews spent 86 days dismantling the wheel. It was used at two more events, but the company failed and George Ferris died in 1896. The wheel originally stood just west of Woodlawn Avenue. In the early 2000s, the city built the Midway Plaisance ice rink on that section of lawn, and **excavation uncovered the original wheel foundations, still in place after more than a century**.

The Midway also included racist displays described as anthropological exhibits. People brought from Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and the Americas were placed in so-called villages and presented to paying crowds as objects of study. The Chicago Tribune promoted the displays as a way to descend the spiral of evolution. These exhibits operated on this lawn throughout the fair.

The sunken shape of the Midway comes from Olmsted's 1871 plan. **He intended to build a canal through this area connecting the Jackson Park lagoons with Washington Park one mile west**. Construction began, but funding ended before water was added. The excavated channel remained as a long lawn.

**The unfinished channel later became a boundary between neighborhoods**. The university and largely white Hyde Park stood north of the Midway, while Woodlawn was to the south. During the Great Migration, the Black Belt along State Street became severely overcrowded, and Black families looked for housing farther east and south. The blocks below the Midway became a major point of pressure. For much of the twentieth century, a person's side of the lawn affected access to mortgages, rent levels, and the value assigned to a block. The racial separation remained clear for decades and was still visible in 1980 between blocks north and south of the Midway.

That boundary resulted from written policies rather than geography. The following stops identify the people and documents that enforced it. **In 1937, about a mile southwest of here, the Hansberry family bought a brick three-flat across one of those lines**. A white mob gathered outside their windows on the first evening. Their daughter Lorraine later adapted the family's experience into A Raisin in the Sun. The house is stop twelve, an optional detour, where the tour explains the covenant used against the family.

stops.title: Rockefeller Chapel
stops.dek: The university's tallest building replaced a row of homes
transcript: Rockefeller Chapel was completed in 1928 and remains the tallest building owned by the university. John D. Rockefeller, the oil baron, **requested that the chapel be the university's central and dominant feature** when he made his final gift to the school. Architect Bertram Goodhue designed a 207-foot tower so the chapel would define the campus skyline. A later member of the Rockefeller family funded one of the world's largest carillons for the tower, containing 72 bells cast in England.

The construction photograph shows a derrick above the unfinished tower and older buildings along the left side of the block. Building the chapel required **demolishing a row of homes on Woodlawn Avenue**. It was one part of a larger expansion between 1926 and 1933, when the campus nearly doubled with twenty-one new Gothic buildings. Most of that land had previously contained homes or other buildings. The university became the largest landowner on the South Side through a series of purchases, sometimes made without identifying the university as the buyer. In one case, title was placed under the name of the university's architect so sellers would not know who was assembling the property.

The same pattern continued over time. A row of homes was removed for the chapel in 1928. Temporary housing for veterans filled the Midway in 1946. During the 1950s, a forty-one-acre campus expansion moved south of the Midway despite objections from residents. University hospitals acquired additional blocks in the 1990s and 2000s. Some of these projects provided important benefits, but the underlying land-use pattern was consistent. When the university needed property, it generally obtained it, and existing residents or institutions moved. The final stops show what happened when that power was applied to a much larger part of the neighborhood.

stops.title: The Robie House
stops.dek: The organizations and rules used to keep Hyde Park white
transcript: Frederick Robie manufactured bicycle parts and managed his father's supply company. **In 1908, at age twenty-eight, he gave Frank Lloyd Wright, the nationally renowned architect, a practical set of requirements for a new home**. He did not want closed, box-shaped rooms or drafts, and he wanted views of the street without giving neighbors a clear view inside. Wright completed the house in 1910 using long Roman brick and extended cantilevered roofs. He called the style Prairie, although many neighbors considered the design unusual.

The Robie House also reflects the wealth of this part of Hyde Park. After the university opened in 1892, professors, deans, and executives built large homes on the surrounding blocks, often on land purchased from Marshall Field. Woodlawn Avenue became one of the neighborhood's most expensive residential streets. The detailed porches and stonework nearby show what residents could afford. Hiring one of the country's most innovative architects was within reach for this community and matched the wealthy residents Paul Cornell had originally hoped to attract.

The house nearly faced demolition twice. In 1941, the neighboring seminary announced plans to remove it, but a letter-writing campaign stopped the project. The seminary tried again in 1957. Frank Lloyd Wright, then ninety, called it the finest house he had designed, and Carl Sandburg compared demolition advocates to book burners. **William Zeckendorf, the developer rebuilding 55th Street on cleared urban renewal land, purchased the house**, used it as his project office, and later transferred it to the university. A developer involved in large-scale neighborhood demolition therefore preserved Hyde Park's best-known house. The building is now a World Heritage Site.

The surrounding blocks also became an early center of organized housing discrimination. The direct question was how wealthy white residents could keep Hyde Park segregated. In **1908, the same year Robie hired Wright**, a Hyde Park lawyer created a neighborhood association for that purpose. The first red box explains how the organization worked.

Neighborhood clubs could pressure sellers and boycott agents, but their influence was mainly local. Real estate organizations expanded the policy by making racial exclusion part of professional rules. Sixteen years later, the national association representing real estate agents included the color line in its code of ethics. The second red box prints that provision in full and identifies the association's Chicago address.

interrupts.title: The improvement associations
body: An improvement association was **a homeowners' organization created to control who could live on particular blocks**. These groups existed before formal deed restrictions, and Hyde Park developed an influential example. In the **autumn of 1908**, attorney Francis Harper organized the **Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club** with 350 members and an openly stated goal of maintaining the color line. Black doctors, teachers, and business owners had already lived in Hyde Park for about fifteen years, but the club targeted them. Members promised to **blacklist realtors who sold to Black buyers**, purchase homes from Black owners, and replace Black employees with white workers. About a decade later, the neighborhood's Property Owners' Journal stated the argument directly: **"Every colored man who moves into Hyde Park knows that he is damaging his white neighbors' property. Therefore, he is making war on the white man."** Educator Fannie Barrier Williams, the first Black woman admitted to the Chicago Woman's Club, was among the established residents the club tried to remove. She remained in the neighborhood.

Violence was used when pressure and paperwork did not succeed. Between **July 1917 and March 1921, white Chicagoans carried out fifty-eight bombings** at the homes of Black families and the offices of agents who sold property to them. Black banker **Jesse Binga** was one of the targets. He continued issuing mortgages and told the commission investigating the attacks, **"I will not run. The race is at stake and not myself."** Only two of the forty families whose homes were bombed moved away. The methods developed by local improvement associations later became national policy. Sixteen years after the Hyde Park club formed, a national realtors' code placed the same racial rule in writing.

interrupts.title: The realtors' rulebook
body: The term **Realtor** refers to membership in a trade association rather than to the occupation itself. The association created the term in 1916, and for twenty-six years its written ethics treated the sale of a house to a Black family in a white neighborhood as a violation. On **June 6, 1924**, the **National Association of Real Estate Boards adopted Article 34** of its Code of Ethics: **"A Realtor should never be instrumental in introducing into a neighborhood a character of property or occupancy, members of any race or nationality, or any individuals whose presence will clearly be detrimental to property values in that neighborhood."** The booklet listed the association's address as **310 South Michigan Avenue, Chicago**, about seven miles north of this block. Its bylaws required each member board to adopt the code, allowed discipline for violations, and permitted the national association to expel boards that refused to enforce it.

Chicago's real estate industry had already adopted similar policies. In **1917, the Chicago Real Estate Board** approved a plan to fill the city **block by block**, and on **May 4, 1921**, it voted to expel members who sold to Black buyers on all-white blocks. Real estate education repeated the same claim. **Frederick Babcock's 1924 Appraisal of Real Estate** stated that "residential values are affected by racial and religious factors." Babcock joined the **Federal Housing Administration in 1934**, led its underwriting division, and saw the federal government's 1938 manual restate his ideas. Explicit racial language was removed from the national code in **1950**, two years after the Supreme Court made restrictive covenants unenforceable. The national realtors' association apologized for this history on **November 19, 2020**.

stops.title: The University of Chicago
stops.dek: A new university designed to appear centuries old
transcript: **The building with the pointed entrance arch is Cobb Hall, the university's first building**. Classes began there on October 1, 1892, with 594 students while the fairgrounds were still under construction one mile east. Silas Cobb, a Chicago harness manufacturer who had arrived in the city nearly penniless sixty years earlier, funded the building. Architect Henry Ives Cobb designed it, although the two men were not related.

This is the second institution in Chicago to use the University of Chicago name. The first was a Baptist school founded in the 1850s at 35th Street and Cottage Grove Avenue on ten acres donated by Senator Stephen Douglas. Douglas was the same person who advised Paul Cornell to invest south of the city, and part of his wealth came from a Mississippi plantation worked by enslaved people. The first university went bankrupt in 1886. When Baptist leaders organized a replacement, they planned a much larger institution. **John D. Rockefeller pledged $600,000** if other donors raised another $400,000, and department store owner Marshall Field donated the first ten acres at this location. Rockefeller's total gifts eventually exceeded $35 million, helping a seminary project become one of the wealthiest universities in the world.

Although the campus was new in the 1890s, the trustees selected **English Gothic architecture modeled on Oxford and Cambridge** so the university would appear much older. Ivy was planted along the walls to strengthen the impression of an established institution with centuries of history.

Despite the Oxford-style buildings, the university served mainly local students for many years. Many lived at home and traveled to campus by train or streetcar because campus housing was too expensive for their families. **Forty-seven percent of the entering class in 1928 lived at home, and by 1940 the figure had reached sixty percent.** Even though the university depended heavily on Chicago residents, one of its own professors could not find housing in Hyde Park.

**In 1942, the university hired William Allison Davis, whose salary was supported by a Rosenwald grant**. He became **the first Black scholar to receive tenure at a major white university**. However, Davis and his family could not rent a home in Hyde Park or Kenwood because of the neighborhood's racial restrictions. He traveled home each night to Washington Park, across a boundary that the university had helped defend in court. The faculty club also refused him membership for several years.

Davis was excluded by formal rules rather than by an informal misunderstanding. Landlords and real estate agents in Hyde Park followed the written code discussed at the previous stop. The university could hire Davis as a leading scholar but could not provide housing for him in the surrounding neighborhood because real estate professionals enforced that rule.

The university also built its early national reputation through football. It helped found the conference that became the Big Ten, and coach Amos Alonzo Stagg was the first college football coach in the country appointed with faculty rank. The team practiced on the Midway and played at a stadium two blocks north of this quadrangle. The next stop covers that stadium and the scientific experiment later conducted beneath its stands.

stops.title: Stagg Field and the pile
stops.dek: A football stadium later became the site of the first nuclear chain reaction
transcript: **The block behind the bronze sculpture, extending east to University Avenue, once contained Stagg Field**. The stadium had castle-like stone walls and round towers. On major fall Saturdays, crowds approaching fifty thousand arrived by train to watch the Maroons, then one of the country's strongest football teams. The 1905 team was undefeated and outscored its opponents 271 to 5. Football first made the university widely known. The photograph on this page shows the field around 1900 before permanent stands were built, with the university quadrangles behind it.

**Robert Maynard Hutchins, who became university president in 1929, believed major college athletics did not belong at a serious academic institution**. In December 1939, he eliminated varsity football, and Chicago later left the Big Ten. The decision weakened alumni support and fundraising. By fall 1953, the College enrolled fewer than thirteen hundred students, and the entering class was less than half the size it had been twenty years earlier. Hutchins instead developed the great-books Core that still shapes undergraduate education. On housing discrimination, however, his administration allowed restrictive covenants to continue even though faculty members described them as morally repulsive. The university's later urban renewal campaign on 55th Street emerged during this period of financial weakness and concern about the neighborhood.

After football ended, the empty stadium was used for a major wartime experiment. In 1942, the Manhattan Project planned to build its first reactor in a forest preserve southwest of Chicago because the work was considered dangerous. A construction strike delayed that site, so Enrico Fermi persuaded project leaders to use a **squash court beneath the west stands of Stagg Field**, a room thirty feet wide and sixty feet long with a balcony at one end. On December 2, 1942, his team withdrew control rods from a stack of graphite and uranium and produced the **first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in history**. The reactor became critical at 3:25 p.m. and was shut down twenty-eight minutes later. The experiment took place secretly in a residential neighborhood of a city with more than three million residents, and even Chicago's mayor was not informed.

The stadium was demolished in 1957, but markers identify the exact location of the experiment. **Henry Moore's Nuclear Energy was installed here on December 2, 1967, exactly twenty-five years later.** The sculpture is about twelve feet tall and stands on a granite plaza. Moore explained that its upper section resembles both a mushroom cloud and a human skull, while the openings below have an architectural form similar to a cathedral interior. From different sides, the sculpture emphasizes those different shapes. The federal government designated the location as the Site of the First Self-Sustaining Nuclear Reaction and a National Historic Landmark. The official plaques are set into the plaza.

**The Regenstein Library, completed in 1970, stands behind the sculpture on the former playing field**. Next to it is **the glass-domed Mansueto Library, which opened in 2011 and stores three and a half million books in a robotic underground vault** fifty feet below the surface. Scientific research gave the university an international reputation, and libraries now occupy the site. At the same time, university lawyers and planners were reshaping the surrounding neighborhood, which is the subject of the remaining stops.

stops.title: The Hansberry house
stops.dek: The Hansberry family's move challenged a restrictive covenant
transcript: This optional stop is included because the brick three-flat in front of you played an important role in the legal fight against housing segregation. The building stands on a quiet block in the Washington Park Subdivision at the northwest edge of Woodlawn. In 1937, the Hansberry family moved here, and their experience later became part of a landmark Supreme Court case. Their daughter Lorraine also drew on what happened in this house when she wrote for Broadway.

**Carl Hansberry moved north from Mississippi during the Great Migration and became a real estate broker**. He saw Black families pay much more for inferior housing because racial restrictions limited where they could buy. **This block was part of the Washington Park Subdivision, a twelve-block area built on the former Washington Park Race Track**, one street south of the park. **Its covenant was signed on September 30, 1927, recorded the following February, and written to remain in effect until January 1, 1948**. It prohibited owners from selling or renting to Black people except live-in servants. The University of Chicago had helped defend the same covenant in court four years before Hansberry arrived. He intentionally selected this area as a test and later wrote in the Chicago Defender, "I figured the most vulnerable spot to attack the restrictive covenants was where the pressure was the greatest."

Hansberry purchased the building in spring 1937 and moved his family into it. **A white mob gathered outside, and an object thrown through a window nearly struck his seven-year-old daughter, Lorraine**. Neighbor Anna Lee sued to enforce the covenant, and **Hansberry v. Lee** reached the United States Supreme Court. The covenant required signatures from owners of **95 percent of the subdivision's street frontage**. An earlier case had accepted that the requirement was met without verifying the signatures, but Hansberry's attorneys showed that the actual percentage was much lower. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled for the family because they could not be bound by an earlier judgment in a case where no one had represented their interests. The decision did not invalidate racial covenants generally, but it made this covenant unenforceable. The Chicago Defender reported that hundreds of homes became available to Black buyers. A nationwide ruling against enforcement came eight years later, but this case was an important earlier challenge.

Carl Hansberry's record was complicated. He challenged racial covenants, sued a railroad over segregated railcars, published pamphlets explaining legal rights, and helped establish one of Chicago's first Black-owned banks. He also earned part of his income by dividing buildings into small kitchenettes, the one-room apartments described later on Drexel Boulevard. City officials accused the family of operating slums and repeatedly fined their properties, while Black newspapers described Hansberry as a committed race leader. Both views reflected a housing market in which Black landlords and tenants had few legal or financial alternatives. Discouraged by the situation, Hansberry was preparing to move to Mexico when he died there in 1946.

Lorraine Hansberry later used the family's experience in her work. **Her 1959 play A Raisin in the Sun follows a Black family considering a move into a white neighborhood where residents do not want them**. It became the first play by a Black woman produced on Broadway. The hostility outside this house and the financial pressure of kitchenette housing both appear in the play. It opened while urban renewal demolition was already taking place elsewhere in Hyde Park.

interrupts.title: Restrictive covenants
body: A racial covenant was **a restriction written into a property deed that prohibited sale or rental to a Black person**. Because the promise applied to later owners, one neighborhood campaign could restrict a block for decades. Covenants spread during the 1910s. In **1926, the Supreme Court allowed them to remain in Corrigan v. Buckley** because the Court treated them as private agreements between property owners.

In **1927, the Chicago Real Estate Board distributed a model racial covenant** drafted by Nathan William MacChesney, counsel for the national association. Churches, clubs, and property owners' groups promoted it block by block. The text stated: **"No part of said premises shall in any manner be used or occupied directly or indirectly by any negro or negroes,"** while exempting janitors, chauffeurs, and domestic servants employed on the property. More than **220 subdivisions in Cook County** adopted similar language. One estimate found that covenants covered **38 of Chicago's 85 square miles of residential land south of North Avenue**. Within a year, the Hyde Park Herald described the network as **"like a marvelous delicately woven chain of armor"** across the South Side.

The University of Chicago financially supported that system. It funded property owners' groups that organized covenant campaigns around campus, quietly helped pay for a 1933 lawsuit that excluded Black families near Washington Park, and spent **tens of thousands of dollars defending covenants in court**. University sociologist Louis Wirth objected and called the restrictions morally repulsive. The covenant on this building came from the campaign the university supported.

When **Carl Hansberry purchased 6140 South Rhodes Avenue** in 1937, a piece of concrete thrown through the window nearly hit seven-year-old Lorraine. In **1940**, the Supreme Court allowed the family to remain because of a procedural defect in the earlier case. In **1948, Shelley v. Kraemer made racial covenants unenforceable throughout the United States**. The language was not automatically removed from existing documents, so racist clauses remain in many Cook County deeds, including some near this location.

stops.title: Daley's Restaurant
stops.dek: Chicago's oldest restaurant has operated near this corner since 1892
transcript: In 1892, Irish immigrant and ironworker **John Daley opened a lunchroom at 63rd Street and Cottage Grove Avenue**. It served crews building the elevated railway while the World's Fair was under construction one mile east. By most accounts, this makes Daley's **the oldest restaurant in Chicago**, older than the elevated trains it originally served. In 1918, Daley sold the business to two Greek immigrants who worked there, waiter Tom Kyros and cook Paul Emmanuel. Their extended family has operated it ever since and kept the Daley name because it was already well established.

In 1932, Kyros and Emmanuel demolished the original building to construct a new restaurant, but their bank failed during construction. The property remained vacant for five years while they worked elsewhere and saved money, and Daley's reopened in 1937. It then remained in business as 63rd Street developed into one of the busiest commercial corridors in Black Chicago. The menu changed with the neighborhood and added dishes such as smothered pork chops, catfish, and biscuits. **Muhammad Ali ate here between training sessions** during the 1960s. Even as disinvestment affected 63rd Street and part of the elevated line was removed, Daley's continued operating. In 2019, it moved across the street to a new building at 6257 South Cottage Grove Avenue.

Daley's is modest compared with the legal and planning systems covered in this tour, but its long history matters. It served the people who entered, changed its menu with the neighborhood, and survived longer than nearly every other business discussed here. After this stop, continue north to Drexel Boulevard, the last of the three optional detours, where the tour explains the housing contracts. The main route then resumes at 55th Street with urban renewal.

stops.title: Drexel Boulevard
stops.dek: One mile of Drexel Boulevard shows the neighborhood's major housing changes
transcript: Stand near the fountain in Drexel Square and look north along the boulevard. For about forty years, this was considered the leading residential address on the South Side and marked the northwest corner of Hyde Park. The buildings along the street show, in sequence, many of the changes described throughout this tour, which is why the detour is included.

Drexel Boulevard was created under the same 1869 law that established the South Park system. Paul Cornell helped lead the campaign for that park system and served on its first board of commissioners. Drexel Boulevard was the first privately owned land purchased by the commission. The Drexel family, Philadelphia bankers who were already subdividing property in the area, had given the city land for the earlier Drexel Avenue at least twenty years before. **The boulevard widened the avenue to one hundred feet and extended it from Oakland Boulevard to Washington Park**. A landscaped median separated carriageways on both sides, creating a scenic route designed for slow travel.

The Drexel family attached its name to the boulevard and honored its father with a monument. **In 1881, the South Park Commissioners accepted a $40,000 fountain** from Francis A. and Anthony J. Drexel in memory of their father, Francis M. Drexel, a banker and land speculator who had never lived in Chicago. Henry Manger designed the fountain, which was installed here in 1882. It is the **oldest public sculpture still standing in a Chicago park**, older than the statues in Lincoln Park and the fountains downtown, and it has remained on this triangular site since Paul Cornell's lifetime.

Wealthy Chicagoans soon built homes on both sides of the boulevard, including many people connected to the stockyards one mile west. Lumber businessman Martin Ryerson built a house here in 1887. In 1891, Dr. **John McGill completed a forty-thousand-square-foot French chateau at 4938 South Drexel**, designed by Henry Ives Cobb, the architect of Cobb Hall. The park commission maintained the median with the care of a private estate. In 1938, it still planted **thirty-nine annual flower beds covering more than fifteen thousand square feet**, more than on any other South Side boulevard. Kenwood, the neighborhood facing this street, was often called the Lake Forest of the South Side because of its wealth and large homes.

The boulevard's first major changes were driven by cost rather than race. Large houses such as the McGill chateau were expensive to maintain. The elevated railroad reached 42nd Street in 1910, opening new areas to development, while wealthy residents increasingly preferred the lakefront north of downtown. During the 1910s and 1920s, many mansions were demolished for apartment buildings or divided into several units. The McGill chateau now contains apartments. The seven-story Sutherland building opened at 4659 South Drexel in 1919. A street originally built for about sixty families was redesigned to house several thousand residents.

In 1948, courts could no longer enforce the racial covenants that had restricted Black families to the crowded Black Belt along State Street. Black buyers could begin purchasing property outside that area, especially along neighborhood edges where white residents were already leaving. Drexel Boulevard was one of those edges. Instead of equal access to ordinary housing finance, many buyers encountered a speculative market prepared to profit from the transition.

Many buildings were then divided into increasingly smaller apartments. Mansions that had already been converted into flats were split again into single rooms with a hot plate and a bathroom shared by residents along the hallway. These units were called kitchenettes. More units allowed landlords to collect more rent from the same building. The resulting crowding and deterioration were later used to support racist claims about Black residents, often by the same people who profited from the rents.

Home purchases were often even more costly. Most banks in Black neighborhoods refused to issue conventional mortgages, so speculators who had bought properties cheaply resold them through installment contracts at prices they set themselves. Contract sales transferred more wealth out of Black Chicago than any other housing method discussed on this tour. The red box below explains the terms and consequences.

The boulevard also became an important center of Black culture. **At 4659 South Drexel, the Sutherland building integrated in 1952 under new ownership and was listed in the Green Book used by Black travelers.** **Its ground-floor Sutherland Lounge became one of the country's leading jazz venues**. Performers included Thelonious Monk, John Coltrane, Louis Armstrong, and Miles Davis. Civil rights meetings were held upstairs. A street originally developed to exclude Black residents became a major performance and organizing site during the 1950s.

Walk north for several blocks before returning to the main route. Notice the cornices, the number of doorbells at each entrance, and which buildings remain single-family homes. Susan O'Connor Davis describes the boulevard building by building in Chicago's Historic Hyde Park. After exploring the street, return southeast to 55th Street, where the main route covers urban renewal.

interrupts.title: Blockbusting
body: Blockbusting expanded after the Supreme Court ended court enforcement of racial covenants in 1948. Real estate operators who had profited from segregation found a new way to profit from neighborhood integration. Blockbusting was **the practice of turning white fear into financial gain**. Speculators repeatedly called white homeowners in the evening and placed flyers under doors, warning that Black families were moving nearby and property values would collapse. A house might be purchased from a white owner for **$12,000** and then resold days or weeks later to a Black family for **$22,000 through a contract sale**, because redlining had made conventional mortgages unavailable.

The system depended on two forms of discrimination. White sellers were encouraged to believe that Black neighbors would destroy property values, while Black buyers had so few housing choices that they were willing to pay far more than the market price. The white seller received less than the property was worth, the Black buyer paid an inflated price, and the speculator kept the difference. The process changed many South Side blocks within only a few years.

interrupts.title: Buying on contract
body: A contract sale was **an installment agreement that offered few protections of renting while delaying the rights of ownership**. Buyers made a down payment and monthly payments but **received no ownership interest until the final payment**. If one payment was missed, the seller could evict the family, keep all previous payments, and resell the same home through another contract. Duke researchers estimate that **75 to 95 percent of homes purchased by Black Chicago families during the 1950s and 1960s were sold on contract**, with an average price markup of **84 percent**. A 1962 Chicago Commission on Human Relations study of four Englewood blocks found that 88 percent of Black home purchases used contracts and included an average 73 percent markup. Sellers were often investment groups made up of downtown professionals, and **the same banks that denied mortgages to the buyers often financed the sellers**.

Attorney **Mark Satter** began investigating contract sales after clients Sally and Albert Bolton made regular payments for two years, missed one deadline, and received an eviction notice. He found that they had paid **three times the amount their seller had paid for the property**. Satter spent the remainder of his life identifying contract sellers and describing the relationship between bank discrimination and speculation. He wrote that banking policy and "the wicked speculators exacted a fearful tribute from the Negro man and his family." Satter died at age forty-nine, and the Chicago Daily News noted that he challenged money lenders when many other lawyers would not.

Black buyers later organized collectively against the system. In the late 1960s, West Side families formed the **Contract Buyers League**, confronted sellers as a group, and placed payments in escrow during a contract strike that continued through January 1970. **More than 400 contracts were renegotiated**, returning about six million dollars in value at the time. The Duke study estimates that contract sales extracted a total of **$3.2 billion to $4 billion** from Black Chicago families.

stops.title: Fifty-Fifth Street
stops.dek: After covenants became unenforceable, speculation was followed by urban renewal
transcript: In 1948, the Supreme Court made racial covenants unenforceable. Black families who had been restricted to the overcrowded Black Belt could then purchase homes on blocks in Hyde Park and Kenwood. In 1950, the combined population of the two neighborhoods was about six percent nonwhite. By 1956, it was almost thirty-seven percent. During those six years, about twenty thousand white residents left and twenty-four thousand Black residents arrived. Many new buyers encountered a coordinated real estate business that operated across entire blocks.

The business depended on two connected practices. Speculators first pressured white owners to sell cheaply by making repeated evening phone calls and distributing alarming flyers about Black families moving nearby. They then resold the same properties to Black buyers at nearly twice the price, usually through installment contracts rather than mortgages because mainstream South Side banks refused to lend to them. Owners also divided buildings into single rooms with hot plates and shared bathrooms to collect more rent. The resulting crowding was then used to support the racist claim that Black residents damaged neighborhoods. The optional Drexel Boulevard stop explains blockbusting and contract sales in more detail. The red box below explains why ordinary mortgages were unavailable.

**Hyde Park residents organized more than sixty volunteer block clubs at the height of the transition**. Members reported illegal apartment conversions, responded to blockbusting calls and flyers, supported homeowners under pressure to sell, and in at least one case **collected money to help a Black family keep a home purchased through a punitive contract**. Their work challenged a financial system already supported by federal lending policy.

The photographs show how 55th Street looked before the present concrete buildings were constructed. Bars, clubs, stores, and other small businesses lined 55th Street and Lake Park Avenue, and the number of taverns increased as the covenants weakened. In 1955, the Compass Players opened at 1152 East 55th Street. The company later developed into Second City. The street was crowded, active, newly integrated, and somewhat rough, but it was also one of Chicago's busiest neighborhood commercial areas.

The University of Chicago viewed the conditions on 55th Street as a threat to its future and used urban renewal law to replace much of the area. The red box below explains the legal power involved, and the remaining narration describes how the university obtained and used it.

By 1950, the university faced serious financial and enrollment problems. The reforms associated with Robert Hutchins had reduced the College to fewer than thirteen hundred students, and trustees considered moving the institution out of Chicago. Relocation was impractical because no buyer was likely to purchase the existing campus. **President Lawrence Kimpton therefore concluded that the surrounding neighborhood would have to change**. In 1952, after a faculty member's wife was kidnapped from her home and one thousand residents attended a protest meeting, **the university created the South East Chicago Commission**. **Attorney Julian Levi led the organization for nearly thirty years, and many residents viewed it as the university's political arm**.

Levi helped develop the state and federal laws later used for urban renewal. **An Illinois law supported by the university in 1953 allowed a private organization to target blocks that might become blighted**. One early project area near campus contained many Japanese American families who had resettled in Chicago after wartime incarceration, along with Black families whose block clubs reported that their buildings were in good condition. Sociologist St. Clair Drake, coauthor of Black Metropolis and a resident of the area, joined a lawsuit opposing the plan. The project proceeded, making Hyde Park and Kenwood the site of the **first major federally supported urban renewal program in the country**. Demolition began near 55th Street and Lake Park Avenue in 1955, and **City Council approved the complete plan on November 7, 1958**. **Nearly four thousand families were displaced**. Sociologists Peter Rossi and Robert Dentler found that displaced white families were much more likely than displaced Black families to find new housing within Hyde Park and Kenwood. James Baldwin later summarized similar programs by saying that urban renewal meant Negro removal, while planners continued to use the terms renewal and conservation.

The two photographs show a commercial street replaced by a shopping center and parking lot. **Most businesses that had operated on 55th Street never reopened.** Renters received moving assistance, but tenant businesses did not. Anderson Hardware was forced to relocate three times. During one rushed move, customers used shopping carts to carry the store's inventory. New construction depended on mortgage financing, which favored national chains such as Woolworth and Walgreens, along with a candy store and burger restaurant. Jane Jacobs was writing The Death and Life of Great American Cities during the same period and used Hyde Park as an example of the problems created when one institution controlled neighborhood development.

The buildings visible from this corner replaced the older 55th Street corridor. **The two concrete towers standing in the center of the road are I. M. Pei's University Apartments**, a 540-unit development completed in 1961. The street was divided around the towers to slow traffic. The lower rows of housing behind small fenced yards were built at the same time. A commercial street of smaller buildings and lower rents became a planned development with larger buildings and higher costs.

**The renewal plan also created the University Neighborhood Homes**, the long buff-brick townhouses designed by Harry Weese and I. M. Pei and built along Lake Park Avenue between 1958 and 1961. It also created parkland. **Nichols Park**, two blocks north along Kimbark Avenue between 53rd and 55th Streets, occupies six acres of cleared blocks purchased by the Park District in **1964 from the Department of Urban Renewal**. Some demolished buildings had housed Japanese American families who moved to Chicago after being unable to return to the West Coast following wartime incarceration. **The park is named for John Fountain Nichols, a Hyde Park artist who worked for the Department of Urban Renewal** and drew plans for his own neighborhood. The Park District's history of the site records how the land was obtained, and the park is now used daily by neighborhood families.

This block shows the full sequence of urban renewal, from legal authority and demolition to replacement development. The final main-route stop is two blocks north and explains how neighborhood residents responded.

interrupts.title: Redlining
body: Redlining was **the practice of grading neighborhoods for lending risk according to race**. In 1939 and 1940, the federal **Home Owners' Loan Corporation** mapped Chicago neighborhoods using four categories: green, blue, yellow, and red, from lowest to highest perceived risk. Federal officials relied heavily on surveys completed by **local real estate agents and lenders** who had been trained with race-based appraisal manuals. The presence of only **three or four Black families could cause an entire neighborhood to be labeled hazardous**. Most of the Black Belt received red grades. Hyde Park and Kenwood were graded yellow, or definitely declining, partly because they bordered Black neighborhoods.

The **Federal Housing Administration** reinforced the same policy. Its 1938 underwriting manual reflected the ideas of **Frederick Babcock**, whose appraisal textbook was discussed at the Robie House. The manual instructed appraisers to identify **"incompatible racial and social groups"** and claimed that property values depended on maintaining the same racial occupancy. It also recommended deed restrictions including **"prohibition of the occupancy of properties except by the race for which they are intended."** A red or yellow rating could block conventional mortgages, home improvement loans, and business loans for every property on a block. According to historians in The Shame of Chicago, when the NAACP asked President Franklin Roosevelt to intervene, the administration responded that the market had to be respected.

The effect on lending was nearly complete. Black realtor **Dempsey Travis** surveyed 243 white-owned Chicago banks and found that **only one would lend to a Black family purchasing in a white neighborhood**. Hyde Park residents responded by creating a **savings and loan in 1952 with contributions from 750 small donors**, allowing Black borrowers to obtain standard mortgages and rehabilitation loans. In most other areas, the absence of bank lending created an opportunity for speculators and contract sellers.

interrupts.title: Urban renewal
body: Urban renewal provided **the legal authority to label areas blighted, clear them with public funds, and select new development for the land**. The **Hyde Park-Kenwood plan, approved on November 7, 1958, was the first large federally supported urban renewal program in the country**. The university's South East Chicago Commission drove the project. An Illinois conservation law passed in 1953 with university support also allowed planners to condemn areas that only **might become blighted in the future**. Public agencies spent about **$40 million acquiring and clearing land**, which was later sold to developers for about $4 million.

The plan produced the townhouses, towers in the center of 55th Street, and the shopping center two blocks north. It removed lower-cost housing and **most of the small businesses on 55th Street**, including taverns, bars, and a neighborhood hardware store. Nearly **four thousand families were displaced**, while the new housing was priced for residents with higher incomes. The university opposed public housing within the renewal area, and **only 34 public housing units were built**. Planners used the terms conservation and renewal, but the program continued a longer pattern in which neighborhood organizations, professional codes, deed restrictions, lending maps, and demolition were used to determine who could live in Hyde Park.
