stops.title: Harper Court
stops.dek: The route ends close to where Hyde Park's development began
transcript: This corner is two blocks from Cornell's stone but represents about 170 years of neighborhood history. Its story begins with the World's Fair. In 1891, real estate investor **Frederick C. Gibbs built twenty-six wooden shops** on 57th Street for businesses serving visitors expected in 1893. Architect George Beaumont designed each shop with a central entrance, two large display windows, and a shared roofline decorated with wooden pagodas. The row extended from 56th to 57th Street and from Kenwood Avenue to Stony Island Avenue, only a few minutes from the Illinois Central station used by fair visitors. The shops were inexpensive structures intended mainly for the exposition season.

**The buildings remained after the fair and developed into an arts community.** Painters, writers, sculptors, dancers, and used-book dealers rented the small shops. Sherwood Anderson worked there. Mildred Clark opened a bookstore and lending library in one of the buildings in 1927 and operated it for decades. Surrealist artist Gertrude Abercrombie maintained a studio in the row. For about fifty years, the former fair shops supported an important part of Chicago's artistic community. **The 57th Street Art Fair, still held on these blocks during the first weekend in June, began in 1948** through the work of one of the shopkeepers.

Gibbs died in 1946 at age ninety, and his niece sold the property. Later owners failed to maintain the buildings. In **May 1962, the Land Clearance Commission purchased the shops for demolition**. Artists held a final festival, and **neighborhood residents then raised funds and obtained Small Business Administration loans to build Harper Court on this corner in 1965**. The new complex offered artisans rents below one hundred dollars a month and was described as a center for the useful arts. **Residents moved the colony's 1893 drinking fountain to the site as a memorial to the original shops.** For about forty years, Harper Court served as a neighborhood gathering place with a folk music club, bookstore, shops, and public benches. In **2007, the University of Chicago purchased Harper Court for $6.8 million**. The complex was demolished and replaced by the glass tower now standing here.

Hyde Park's urban renewal history includes two important outcomes. After renewal, Hyde Park remained one of Chicago's few substantially integrated neighborhoods for several decades, with a population that was roughly one-third Black and one-half white. Many residents worked seriously to preserve that integration. At the same time, the greatest costs of the renewal plan fell on lower-income residents and businesses who had little control over the process. The underlying policy often treated racial integration as acceptable only if poor residents were removed. In 1962, students occupied the university administration building for two weeks after paired Black and white applicants demonstrated that the university was discriminating against Black renters in its own apartment buildings. Bernie Sanders, then twenty years old, chaired the campus organization that conducted the test. The university negotiated an end to the protest and later changed the policy.

The full history begins with Paul Cornell buying marshland and selecting the residents he wanted to attract. Olmsted planned the parks, and the Great Fire destroyed his drawings. The World's Fair impressed millions of visitors while Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass distributed a pamphlet explaining Black exclusion. Wealthy residents later created improvement associations, the real estate industry placed the same rule in its code of ethics, its lawyer drafted restrictive covenants, federal agencies marked lending maps by race, speculators used contract sales on streets such as Drexel Boulevard, and urban renewal cleared much of 55th Street. Each stage resulted from decisions made by identifiable people and institutions rather than from an automatic neighborhood change. More information about Rooted Forward's work is available at rooted-forward.org.
